sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.stage: SCENE: Behind the Orchestra on the right the farmhouse of Trygaeus, in the center the mouth of a cave closed up with huge boulders, on the left the palace of Zeus. In front of the farmhouse is a stable, the door of which is closed. Two of Trygaeus' slaves are seen in front of the stable, one of them kneading cakes of dung, the other taking the finished cakes and throwing them into the stable.
sp.p: Quick, quick, bring the dung-beetle his cake.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: There it is. Give it to him, and may it kill him! And may he never eat a better.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Now give him this other one kneaded up with ass's dung.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: There! I've done that too. And where's what you gave him just now? Surely he can't have devoured it yet!

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Indeed he has; he snatched it, rolled it between his feet and bolted it. Come, hurry up, knead up a lot and knead them stiffly.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: Oh, scavengers, help me in the name of the gods, if you do not wish to see me fall down choked.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Come, come, another made from the stool of a fairy's favorite. That will be to the beetle's taste; he likes it well ground.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: There! I am free at least from suspicion; none will accuse me of tasting what I mix.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Faugh! come, now another! keep on mixing with all your might.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: By god, no. I can stand this awful cesspool stench no longer.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: I shall bring you the whole ill-smelling gear.

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: Pitch it down the sewer sooner, and yourself with it. To the Audience. Maybe, one of you can tell me where I can buy a stopped-up nose, for there is no work more disgusting than to mix food for a dung-beetle and to carry it to him. A pig or a dog will at least pounce upon our excrement without more ado, but this foul wretch affects the disdainful, the spoilt mistress, and won't eat unless I offer him a cake that has been kneaded for an entire day.... But let us open the door a bit ajar without his seeing it. Has he done eating? Come, pluck up courage, cram yourself till you burst! The cursed creature! It wallows in its food! It grips it between its claws like a wrestler clutching his opponent, and with head and feet together rolls up its paste like a rope-maker twisting a hawser. What an indecent, stinking, gluttonous beast! I don't know what angry god let this monster loose upon us, but of a certainty it was neither Aphrodite nor the Graces.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Who was it then?

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: No doubt Zeus, the God of the Thundercrap.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: But perhaps some spectator, some beardless youth, who thinks himself a sage, will say, “What is this? What does the beetle mean?” And then an Ionian, sitting next him, will add, “I think it's an allusion to Cleon, who so shamelessly feeds on filth all by himself.” —

sp.speaker: Second Servant
sp.p: But now I'm going indoors to fetch the beetle a drink.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: As for me, I will explain the matter to you all, children, youths, grown-ups and old men, aye, even to the decrepit dotards. My master is mad, not as you are, but with another sort of madness, quite a new kind. The livelong day he looks open-mouthed towards heaven and never stops addressing Zeus. “Ah! Zeus,” he cries, “what are thy intentions? Lay aside thy besom; do not sweep Greece away!” Ah! Hush, hush! I think I hear his voice!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! Zeus, what art thou going to do for our people? Dost thou not see this, that our cities will soon be but empty husks?

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: As I told you, that is his form of madness. There you have a sample of his follies. When his trouble first began to seize him, he said to himself, “By what means could I go straight to Zeus?” Then he made himself very slender little ladders and so clambered up towards heaven; but he soon came hurtling down again and broke his head. Yesterday, to our misfortune, he went out and brought us back this thoroughbred, but from where I know not, this great beetle, whose groom he has forced me to become. He himself caresses it as though it were a horse, saying, “Oh! my little Pegasus, my noble aerial steed, may your wings soon bear me straight to Zeus!” But what is my master doing? I must stoop down to look through this hole. Oh! great gods! Here! neighbors, run here quick! here is my master flying off mounted on his beetle as if on horseback.

div.stage: The machine brings in Trygaeus astride an enormous figure of a dung beetle with wings spread.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Gently, gently, go easy, beetle; don't start off so proudly, or trust at first too greatly to your powers; wait till you have sweated, till the beating of your wings shall make your limb joints supple. Above all things, don't let off some foul smell. I adjure you; else I would rather have you stay right in the stable.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Poor master! Is he crazy?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Silence! silence!

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: But why start up into the air on chance?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: 'Tis for the weal of all the Greeks; I am attempting a daring and novel feat.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: But what is your purpose? What useless folly!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No words of ill omen! Give vent to joy and command all men to keep silence,to close down their drains and privies with new tiles and to cork up their own arses.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: No, I shall not be silent, unless you tell me where you are going.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why, where am I likely to be going across the sky, if it be not to visit Zeus?

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: For what purpose?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I want to ask him what he reckons to do for all the Greeks.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: And if he doesn't tell you?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I shall pursue him at law as a traitor who sells Greece to the Medes.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Death seize me, if I let you go.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: It is absolutely necessary.

sp.speaker: First Servant
sp.p: Alas! alas! dear little girls, your father is deserting you secretly to go to heaven. Ah! poor orphans, entreat him, beseech him.

div.stage: The little daughters of Trygaeus come out.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: Father! father! what is this I hear? Is it true? What! you would leave me, you would vanish into the sky, you would go to the crows? Impossible!

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: Answer, father, if you love me.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, I am going. You hurt me too sorely, my daughters, when you ask me for bread, calling me your daddy, and there is not the ghost of an obolus in the house; if I succeed and come back, you will have a barley loaf every morning —and a punch in the eye for sauce!

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: But how will you make the journey? There's no ship that will take you there.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, but this winged steed will.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: But what an idea, papa, to harness a beetle, to fly to the gods on.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: We see from Aesop's fables that they alone can fly to the abode of the Immortals.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: Father, father, that's a tale nobody can believe! that such a smelly creature can have gone to the gods.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: It went to have vengeance on the eagle and break its eggs.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: Why not saddle Pegasus? you would have a more tragic appearance in the eyes of the gods.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Eh! don't you see, little fool, that then twice the food would be wanted? Whereas my beetle devours again as filth what I have eaten myself.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: And if it fell into the watery depths of the sea, could it escape with its wings?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I am fitted with a rudder in case of need, and my Naxos beetle will serve me as a boat.

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: And what harbor will you put in at?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why, is there not the harbor of Cantharus at the Piraeus?

sp.speaker: Little Daughter
sp.p: Take care not to knock against anything and so fall off into space; once a cripple, you would be a fit subject for Euripides, who would put you into a tragedy.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.stage: As the Machine hoists him higher.
sp.p: I'll see to it. Good-bye!To the Athenians.You, for love of whom I brave these dangers, do ye neither fart nor crap for the space of three days, for, if, while cleaving the air, my steed should scent anything, he would fling me head foremost from the summit of my hopes.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Now come, my Pegasus, get a-going with up-pricked ears and make your golden bridle resound gaily. Eh! what are you doing? What are you up to? Do you turn your nose towards the cesspools? Come, pluck up a spirit; rush upwards from the earth, stretch out your speedy wings and make straight for the palace of Zeus; for once give up foraging in your daily food. —Hi! you down there, what are you after now? Oh! my god! it's a man taking a crap in the Piraeus, close to the whorehouses. But is it my death you seek then, my death? Will you not bury that right away and pile a great heap of earth upon it and plant wild thyme therein and pour perfumes on it? If I were to fall from up here and misfortune happened to me, the town of Chios would owe a fine of five talents for my death, all because of your damned arse.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Alas! how frightened I am! oh! I have no heart for jests. Ah! machinist, take great care of me. There is already a wind whirling round my navel; take great care or, from sheer fright, I shall form food for my beetle—But I think I am no longer far from the gods; aye, that is the dwelling of Zeus, I perceive.The beetle descends and comes to a halt in front of the house of Zeus. Trygaeus dismounts and knocks at the door.Hullo! Hi! where is the doorkeeper? Will no one open?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I think I can sniff a man.Opening the door. Why, what plague is this?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: A horse-beetle.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! impudent, shameless rascal! oh! scoundrel! triple scoundrel! the greatest scoundrel in the world! how did you come here? Oh! scoundrel of all scoundrels! your name? Reply.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Triple scoundrel.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Your country?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Triple scoundrel.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Your father?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: My father? Triple scoundrel.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: By the Earth, you shall die, unless you tell me your name.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I am Trygaeus of the Athmonian deme, a good vine-dresser, little addicted to quibbling and not at all an informer.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Why do you come?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I come to bring you this meat.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! my good friend, did you have a good journey?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Glutton, be off! I no longer seem a triple scoundrel to you. Come, call Zeus.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! ah! you are a long way yet from reaching the gods, for they moved yesterday.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: To what part of the earth?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Eh! of the earth, did you say?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: In short, where are they then?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Very far, very far, right at the furthest end of the dome of heaven.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But why have they left you all alone here?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I am watching what remains of the furniture, the little pots and pans, the bits of chairs and tables, and odd wine-jars.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And why have the gods moved away?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because of their wrath against the Greeks. They have located War in the house they occupied themselves and have given him full power to do with you exactly as he pleases; then they went as high up as ever they could, so as to see no more of your fights and to hear no more of your prayers.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What reason have they for treating us so?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because they have afforded you an opportunity for peace more than once, but you have always preferred war. If the Laconians got the very slightest advantage, they would exclaim, “By the Twin Brethren! the Athenians shall smart for this.” If, on the contrary, the latter triumphed and the Laconians came with peace proposals, you would say, “By Demeter, they want to deceive us. No, by Zeus, we will not hear a word; they will always be coming as long as we hold Pylos.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, that is quite the style our folk do talk in.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: So that I don't know whether you will ever see Peace again.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why, where has she gone to then?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: War has cast her into a deep pit.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Down there, at the very bottom. And you see what heaps of stones he has piled over the top, so that you should never pull her out again.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Tell me, what is War preparing against us?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: All I know is that last evening he brought along a huge mortar.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And what is he going to do with his mortar?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: He wants to pound up all the cities of Greece in it.... But I must say good-bye, for I think he is coming out; what an uproar he is making!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! great gods let us seek safety; I think I already hear the noise of this fearful war mortar.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Oh! mortals, mortals, wretched mortals, how your jaws will snap!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! divine Apollo! what a prodigious big mortar! Oh, what misery the very sight of War causes me! This then is the foe from whom I fly, who is so cruel, so formidable, so stalwart, so solid on his legs!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Oh! Prasiae! thrice wretched, five times, aye, a thousand times wretched! for thou shalt be destroyed this day.

div.stage: He throws some leeks into the mortar.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: This, gentlemen, does not concern us over much; it's only so much the worse for the Laconians.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Oh! Megara! Megara! how utterly are you going to be ground up! what fine mincemeat are you to be made into!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Alas! alas! what bitter tears there will be among the Megarians!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Oh, Sicily! you too must perish! Your wretched towns shall be grated like this cheese. Now let us pour some Attic honey into the mortar.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! I beseech you! use some other honey; this kind is worth four obols; be careful, oh! be careful of our Attic honey.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Hi! Tumult, you slave there!

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: What do you want?

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Out upon you! Standing there with folded arms! Take this cuff on the head for your pains.

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Oh! how it stings! Master, have you got garlic in your fist, I wonder?

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Run and fetch me a pestle.

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Butwe haven't got one; it was only yesterday we moved.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Go and fetch me one from Athens, and hurry, hurry!

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: I'll hurry; if I return without one, I shall have no cause for laughing.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! what is to become of us, wretched mortals that we are? See the danger that threatens if he returns with the pestle, for War will quietly amuse himself with pounding all the towns of Hellas to pieces. Ah! Bacchus! cause this herald of evil to perish on his road!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Well, what?

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: You have brought back nothing?

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Alas! the Athenians have lost their pestle —the tanner, who ground Greece to powder.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! Athena, venerable mistress! it is well for our city he is dead, and before he could serve us with this hash.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Then go and seek one at Sparta and have done with it!

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Aye, aye, master!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Be back as quick as ever you can.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What is going to happen, friends? This is the critical hour. Ah! if there is some initiate of Samothrace among you, this is surely the moment to wish this messenger some accident —some sprain or strain.

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: Alas! alas! thrice again, alas!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: What is it? Again you come back without it?

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: The Spartans too have lost their pestle.

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: How, varlet?

sp.speaker: Tumult
sp.p: They had lent it to their allies in Thrace, who have lost it for them.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Long life to you, Thracians! My hopes revive, pluck up courage, mortals!

sp.speaker: War
sp.p: Take all this stuff; I am going in to make a pestle for myself.
sp.stage: He goes in, followed by Tumult.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Now is the time to sing as Datis did, as he masturbated at high noon, “Oh pleasure! oh enjoyment! oh delights!” Now, oh Greeks! is the moment when freed of quarrels and fighting, we should rescue sweet Peace and draw her out of this pit, before some other pestle prevents us. Come, laborers, merchants, workmen, artisans, strangers, whether you be domiciled or not, islanders—
Come here, Greeks of all countries, come hurrying here with picks and levers and ropes!This is the moment to drain a cup in honor of the Good Genius.

div.stage: The Chorus enters; it consists of laborers and farmers from various Greek states.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Come hither all! quick, quick, hasten to the rescue! All peoples of Greece, now is the time or never, for you to help each other. You see yourselves freed from battles and all their horrors of bloodshed. The day hateful to Lamachus has come.

Come then, what must be done? Give your orders, direct us, for I swear to work this day without ceasing, until with the help of our levers and our engines we have drawn back into light the greatest of all goddesses, her to whom the olive is so dear.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Silence! if War should hear your shouts of joy he would bound forth from his retreat in fury.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Such a decree overwhelms us with joy; how different to the edict, which bade us muster with provisions for three days.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us beware lest the cursed Cerberus prevent us even from the nethermost hell from delivering the goddess by his furious howling, just as he did when on earth.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Once we have hold of her, none in the world will be able to take her from us. Huzza! huzza!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You will work my death if you don't subdue your shouts. War will come running out and trample everything beneath his feet.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Well then! Let him confound, let him trample, let him overturn everything! We cannot help giving vent to our joy.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! cruel fate! My friends! in the name of the gods, what possess you? Your dancing will wreck the success of a fine undertaking.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: It's not I who want to dance; it's my legs that bound with delight.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Enough, please, cease your gambols.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: There! That's all.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You say so, and nevertheless you go on.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Yet one more figure and it's done.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Well, just this one; then you must dance no more.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: No, no more dancing, if we can help you.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But look, you are not stopping even now.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: By Zeus, I am only throwing up my right leg, that's all.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, I grant you that, but pray, annoy me no further.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Ah! the left leg too will have its fling; well, that's its right. I am so happy, so delighted at not having to carry my buckler any more. I fart for joy and I laugh more than if I had cast my old age, as a serpent does its skin.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, it's not time for joy yet, for you are not sure of success. But when you have got the goddess,

Then rejoice, shout and laugh; thenceforward you will be able to sail or stay at home, to make love or sleep, to attend festivals and processions, to play at cottabos, live like true Sybarites and to shout, Io, io!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Ah! God grant we may see the blessed day. I have suffered so much; have so oft slept with Phormio on hard beds. You will no longer find me a bitter and angry judge, nor, naturally, hard in my ways, as heretofore, but turned indulgent and grown younger by twenty years through happiness. We have been killing ourselves long enough, tiring ourselves out with going to the Lyceum and returning laden with spear and buckler. —But what can we do to please you? Come, speak; for 'tis a good Fate that has named you our leader.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: How shall we set about removing these stones?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Rash reprobate, what do you propose doing?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Nothing bad, as Cillicon said.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You are undone, you wretch.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, if the lot had to decide my life, for Hermes would know how to turn the chance.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You are lost, you are dead.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: On what day?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: This instant.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But I have not provided myself with flour and cheese yet to start for death.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You are kneaded and ground already, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Hah! I have not yet tasted that gentle pleasure.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Don't you know that Zeus has decreed death for him who is caught exhuming Peace?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What! must I really and truly die?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You must.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Well then, lend me three drachmae to buy a young pig; I wish to have myself initiated before I die.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! Zeus, the Thunderer!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I adjure you in the name of the gods, master, don't report us!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I may not, I cannot keep silent.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: In the name of the meats which I brought you so good-naturedly.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Why, wretched man, Zeus will annihilate me, if I do not shout out at the top of my voice, to inform him what you are plotting.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh, no! don't shout, I beg you, dear little Hermes.
And what are you doing, comrades? You stand there as though you were stocks and stones. Wretched men, speak, entreat him at once; otherwise he will be shouting.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! mighty Hermes! do not do it; no, do not do it! If ever you have eaten some young pig, sacrificed by us on your altars, with pleasure, may this offering not be without value in your sight to-day.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Do you not hear them wheedling you, mighty god?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Be not pitiless toward our prayers; permit us to deliver the goddess. Oh! the most human, the most generous of the gods, be favourable toward us, if it be true that you detest the haughty crests and proud brows of Pisander; we shall never cease, oh master, offering you sacred victims and solemn prayers.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Have mercy, mercy, let yourself be touched by their words; never was your worship so dear to them as to-day. Aside.Really they are the greatest thieves that ever were. To Hermes.And I shall reveal to you a great and terrible plot that is being hatched against the gods.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Hah! speak and perchance I shall let myself be softened.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Know then, that the Moon and that infamous Sun are plotting against you, and want to deliver Greece into the hands of the barbarians.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: What for?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Because it is to you that we sacrifice, whereas the barbarians worship them; hence they would like to see you destroyed, that they alone might receive the offerings.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Is it then for this reason that these untrustworthy charioteers have for so long been defrauding us, one of them robbing us of daylight and the other nibbling away at the other's disk?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, certainly. So therefore, Hermes, my friend, help us with your whole heart to find and deliver the captive and we will celebrate the great Panathenaea in your honor as well as all the festivals of the other gods; for Hermes shall be the Mysteries, the Dipolia, the Adonia; everywhere the towns, freed from their miseries, will sacrifice to Hermes the Liberator; you will be loaded with benefits of every kind, and to start with, I offer you this cup for libations as your first present.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! how golden cups do influence me!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come, friends, get to work. To the pit quickly, pick in hand, and drag away the stones.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: We go, but you, cleverest of all the gods, supervise our labours; tell us, good workman as you are, what we must do; we shall obey your orders with alacrity.

sp.stage: They begin to lift the stones.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Quick, reach me your cup, and let us preface our work by addressing prayers to the gods.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Libation! Libation! Silence! Silence!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us offer our libations and our prayers, so that this day may begin an era of unalloyed happiness for Greece and that he who has bravely pulled at the rope with us may never resume his buckler.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Aye, may we pass our lives in peace, caressing our mistresses and poking the fire.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: May he who would prefer the war—

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Be ever drawing barbed arrows out of his elbows, O Lord Dionysus.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: If there be a citizen, greedy for military rank and honors, who refuses, oh, divine Peace! to restore you to daylight—

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: May he behave as cowardly as Cleonymus on the battlefield.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: If a lance-maker or a dealer in shields desires war for the sake of better trade—

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: May he be taken by pirates and eat nothing but barely.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: If some ambitious man does not help us, because he wants to become a General, or if a slave is plotting to pass over to the enemy—

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let his limbs be broken on the wheel, may he be beaten to death with rods!

sp.speaker: Trygaius
sp.p: As for us, may Fortune favour us! Io! Paean, Io!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Don't say Paean, but simply, Io.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Very well, then! Io! Io! I'll simply say, Io! To Hermes, the Graces, the Horae, Aphrodite, Eros! But, to Ares?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: No! No!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Not to Enyalius?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, all strain at the ropes to tear off the cover. Pull!

div.stage: The stones have been removed and a rope attached to the cover of the pit. The indented portions of the following scene are a sort of chanty.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Heave away!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Heave away, heave, heave, oh!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come, pull harder, harder.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Heave away, heave, heave, oh!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Still harder, harder still.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Heave away, heave! Heave away, heave, heave, oh!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, come, there is no working together. Come! all pull at the same instant! you Boeotians are only pretending. Beware!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come, heave away, heave!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Heave away, heave oh!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hi! you two pull as well.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why, I am pulling, I am hanging on to the rope and straining till I am almost off my feet; I am working with all my might.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Why does not the work advance then?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Lamachus, this is terrible! You are in the way, sitting there. We have no use for your Medusa's head, friend.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: But wait, the Argives have not pulled the least bit; they have done nothing but laugh at us for our pains while they were getting gain with both hands.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! my dear sir, the Laconians at all events pull with vigor.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: But look! only those among them who generally hold the plough-tail show any zeal, while the armorers impede them in their efforts.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: And the Megarians too are doing nothing, yet look how they are pulling and showing their teeth like famished curs. They are dying of hunger, by Zeus.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: This won't do, friends. Come! all together! Everyone to the work and with a good heart for the business.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Heave away, heave!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Harder!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Heave away, heave!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come on then, by heaven.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: We are moving it a little.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Isn't it terrible and stupid! some pull one way and others another. You Argives there, beware of a thrashing!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come, put your strength into it.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Heave away, heave!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: There are many ill-disposed folk among us.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Do you at least, who long for peace, pull heartily.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: But there are some who prevent us.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Off to the Devil with you, Megarians! The goddess hates you. She recollects that you were the first to rub her the wrong way. Athenians, you are not well placed for pulling. There you are too busy with law-suits; if you really want to free the goddess, get down a little towards the sea.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Come, friends, none but husbandmen on the rope.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! that will do ever so much better.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: He says the thing is going well. Come, all of you, together and with a will.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: It's the husbandmen who are doing all the work.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Come then, come, and all together!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Hah! hah! at last there is some unanimity in the work.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Don't let us give up, let us redouble our efforts.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: There! now we have it!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Come then, all together! Heave away, heave! Heave away, heave! Heave away, heave! Heave away, heave! Heave away, heave! All together!

sp.stage: Peace is drawn out of the pit. With her come Opora and Theoria.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! venerated goddess, who givest us our grapes, where am I to find the ten-thousand-gallon words wherewith to greet thee? I have none such at home. Oh! hail to thee, Opora, and thee, Theoria! How beautiful is thy face! How sweet thy breath! What gentle fragrance comes from thy bosom, gentle as freedom from military duty, as the most dainty perfumes!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Is it then a smell like a soldier's knapsack?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! hateful soldier! your hideous satchel makes me sick! it stinks like the belching of onions, whereas this lovable deity has the odor of sweet fruits, of festivals, of the Dionysia, of the harmony of flutes, of the tragic poets, of the verses of Sophocles, of the phrases of Euripides—

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: That's a foul calumny, you wretch! She detests that framer of subtleties and quibbles.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: —of ivy, of straining-bags for wine, of bleating ewes, of provision-laden women hastening to the kitchen, of the tipsy servant wench, of the upturned wine-jar, and of a whole heap of other good things.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Then look how the reconciled towns chat pleasantly together, how they laugh, and yet they are all cruelly mishandled; their wounds are bleeding still.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But let us also scan the mien of the spectators; we shall thus find out the trade of each.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Good god!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Do you see that poor crest-maker, tearing at his hair?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: —and that pike-maker, who has just farted in yon sword-cutler's face?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And do you see with what pleasure this sickle-maker is thumbing his nose at the spear-maker?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Now tell the husbandmen to be off.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Listen, good folk! Let the husbandmen take their farming tools and return to their fields as quickly as possible, but without either sword, spear or javelin. All is as quiet as if Peace had been reigning for a century. Come, let everyone go and till the earth, singing the Paean.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh, thou, whom men of standing desired and who art good to husbandmen, I have gazed upon thee with delight; and now I go to greet my vines, to caress after so long an absence the fig trees I planted in my youth.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Friends, let us first adore the goddess, who has delivered us from crests and Gorgons; then let us hurry to our farms, having first bought a nice little piece of salt fish to eat in the fields.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: By Poseidon! what a fine crew they make and dense as the crust of a cake; they are as nimble as guests on their way to a feast.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: See, how their iron spades glitter and how beautifully their three-pronged mattocks glisten in the sun! How regularly they align the plants! I also burn to go into the country and to turn over the earth I have so long neglected. —

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Friends, do you remember the happy life that Peace afforded us formerly; can you recall the splendid baskets of figs, both fresh and dried, the myrtles, the sweet wine, the violets blooming near the spring, and the olives, for which we have wept so much? Worship, adore the goddess for restoring you so many blessings.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hail! hail! thou beloved divinity! thy return overwhelms us with joy. When far from thee, my ardent wish to see my fields again made me pine with regret. From thee came all blessings. Oh! much desired Peace! thou art the sole support of those who spend their lives tilling the earth. Under thy rule we had a thousand delicious enjoyments at our beck; thou wert the husbandman's wheaten cake and his safeguard. So that our vineyards, our young fig-tree woods and all our plantations hail thee with delight and smile at thy coming.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: But where was she then, I wonder, all the long time she spent away from us? Hermes, thou benevolent god, tell us!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Wise husbandmen, hearken to my words, if you want to know why she was lost to you. The start of our misfortunes was the exile of Phidias; Pericles feared he might share his ill-luck, he mistrusted your peevish nature and, to prevent all danger to himself, he threw out that little spark, the Megarian decree, set the city aflame, and blew up the conflagration with a hurricane of war, so that the smoke drew tears from all Greeks both here and over there. At the very outset of this fire our vines were a-crackle, our casks knocked together; it was beyond the power of any man to stop the disaster, and Peace disappeared.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: That, by Apollo! is what no one ever told me; I could not think what connection there could be between Phidias and Peace.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Nor I, until now. This accounts for her beauty, if she is related to him. There are so many things that escape us.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Then, when the towns subject to you saw that you were angered one against the other and were showing each other your teeth like dogs, they hatched a thousand plots to pay you no more dues and gained over the chief citizens of Sparta at the price of gold. They, being as shamelessly greedy as they were faithless in diplomacy, chased off Peace with ignominy to let loose War. Though this was profitable to them, it was the ruin of the husbandmen, who were innocent of all blame; for, in revenge, your galleys went out to devour their figs.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And with justice too; did they not break down my black fig tree, which I had planted and dunged with my own hands?

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Yes, by Zeus! yes, that was well done; the wretches broke a chest for me with stones, which held six medimni of corn.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Then the rural laborers flocked into the city and let themselves be bought over like the others. Not having even a grape-stone to munch and longing after their figs, they looked towards the demagogues. These well knew that the poor were driven to extremity and lacked even bread; but they nevertheless drove away the Goddess, each time she reappeared in answer to the wish of the country, with their loud shrieks that were as sharp as pitchforks; furthermore, they attacked the well-filled purses of the richest among our allieson the pretence that they belonged to Brasidas' party. And then you would tear the poor accused wretch to pieces with your teeth; for the city, all pale with hunger and cowed with terror, gladly snapped up any calumny that was thrown it to devour. So the strangers, seeing what terrible blows the informers dealt, sealed their lips with gold. They grew rich, while you, alas! you could only see that Greece was going to ruin. It was the tanner who was the author of all this woe.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Enough said, Hermes leave that man in Hades, whither he has gone; he no longer belongs to us, but rather to you.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: That he was a cheat, a braggart, a calumniator when alive, why, nothing could be truer; but anything you might say now would be an insult to one of your own folk.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! venerated Goddess! why art thou silent?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: And how could she speak to the spectators? She is too angry at all that they have made her suffer.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: At least let her speak a little to you, Hermes.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Tell me, my dear, what are your feelings with regard to them? Come, you relentless foe of all bucklers, speak; I am listening to you. Peace whispers into Hermes' ear.Is that your grievance against them? Yes, yes, I understand. Hearken, you folk, this is her complaint. She says, that after the affair of Pylos she came to you unbidden to bring you a basket full of truces and that you thrice repulsed her by your votes in the assembly.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, we did wrong, but forgive us, for our mind was then entirely absorbed in leather.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Listen again to what she has just asked me. Who was her greatest foe here? and furthermore, had she a friend who exerted himself to put an end to the fighting?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Her most devoted friend was Cleonymus; it is undisputed.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: How then did Cleonymus behave in fights?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! the bravest of warriors! Only he was not born of the father he claims; he showed it quick enough in the army by throwing away his weapons.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: There is yet another question she has just put to me. Who rules now in the rostrum?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: It's Hyperbolus who now holds empire on the Pnyx. To Peace.What now? you turn away your head!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: She is vexed, that the people should give themselves a wretch of that kind for their chief.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! we shall not employ him again; but the people, seeing themselves without a leader, took him haphazard, just as a man, who is naked, springs upon the first cloak he sees.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: She asks, what will be the result of such a choice by the city?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: We shall be more far-seeing in consequence.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: And why?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Because he is a lamp-maker. Formerly we only directed our business by groping in the dark; now we shall only deliberate by lamplight.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! oh! what questions she does order me to put to you!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What are they?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: She wants to have news of a whole heap of old-fashioned things she left here. First of all, how is Sophocles?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Very well, but something very strange has happened to him.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: He has turned from Sophocles into Simonides.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Into Simonides? How so?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Because, though old and broken-down as he is, he would put to sea on a hurdle to gain an obolus.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: And wise Cratinus, is he still alive?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: He died about the time of the Laconian invasion.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Of a swoon. He could not bear the shock of seeing one of his casks full of wine broken. Ah! what a number of other misfortunes our city has suffered! So, dearest mistress, nothing can now separate us from thee.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: If that be so, receive Opora here for a wife; take her to the country, live with her, and grow fine grapes together.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, my dear one, come and accept my kisses. To Hermes.Tell me, Hermes, my master, do you think it would hurt me to love her a little, after so long an abstinence?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: No, not if you swallow a potion of penny-royal afterwards. But hasten to lead Theoria to the Senate; that was where she lodged before.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! fortunate Senate! Thanks to Theoria, what soups you will swallow for the space of three days! how you will devour meats and cooked tripe! Come, farewell, friend Hermes!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: And to you also, my dear sir, may you have much happiness, and don't forget me.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: >Come, beetle, home, home, and let us fly on a swift wing.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! he is no longer here.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Where has he gone to then?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: He is ‘harnessed to the chariot of Zeus and bears the thunderbolts.’

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But where will the poor wretch get his food?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: He will eat Ganymede's ambrosia.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Very well then, but how am I going to descend?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! never fear, there is nothing simpler; place yourself beside the goddess.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, my pretty maidens, follow me quickly; there are plenty of men waiting for you with their tools ready.He goes out, with Opora and Theoria.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Farewell and good luck be yours! Let us begin by handing over all this gear to the care of our servants, for no place is less safe than a theater; there is always a crowd of thieves prowling around it, seeking to find some mischief to do. Come, keep a good watch over all this. As for ourselves, let us explain to the spectators what we have in our minds, the purpose of our play.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: The Chorus turns and faces the audience.
sp.p: Undoubtedly the comic poet who mounted the stage to praise himself in the parabasis would deserve to be handed over to the sticks of the beadles. Nevertheless, oh Muse, if it be right to esteem the most honest and illustrious of our comic writers at his proper value, permit our poet to say that he thinks he has deserved a glorious renown. First of all, he is the one who has compelled his rivals no longer to scoff at rags or to war with lice; and as for those Heracleses, always chewing and ever hungry, he was the first to cover them with ridicule and to chase them from the stage; he has also dismissed that slave, whom one never failed to set weeping before you, so that his comrade might have the chance of jeering at his stripes and might ask, “Wretch, what has happened to your hide? Has the lash rained an army of its thongs on you and laid your back waste?” After having delivered us from all these wearisome ineptitudes and these low buffooneries, he has built up for us a great art, like a palace with high towers, constructed of fine phrases, great thoughts and of jokes not common on the streets. Moreover it's not obscure private persons or women that he stages in his comedies; but, bold as Heracles, it's the very greatest whom he attacks, undeterred by the fetid stink of leather or the threats of hearts of mud. He has the right to say, “I am the first ever dared to go straight for that beast with the sharp teeth and the terrible eyes that flashed lambent fire like those of Cynna, surrounded by a hundred lewd flatterers, who spittle-licked him to his heart's content; it had a voice like a roaring torrent, the stench of a seal, the unwashed balls of a Lamia and the arse of a camel. I did not recoil in horror at the sight of such a monster, but fought him relentlessly to win your deliverance and that of the islanders.” Such are the services which should be graven in your recollection and entitle me to your thanks. Yet I have not been seen frequenting the wrestling school intoxicated with success and trying to seduce young boys; but I took all my theatrical gear and returned straight home. I pained folk but little and caused them much amusement; my conscience rebuked me for nothing.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: More and more rapidly from here on.
sp.p: Hence both grown men and youths should be on my side and I likewise invite the bald to give me their votes; for, if I triumph, everyone will say, both at table and at festivals, “Carry this to the bald man, give these cakes to the bald one, do not grudge the poet whose talent shines as bright as his own bare skull the share he deserves.”

sp.speaker: First Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Oh, Muse! drive the war far from our city and come to preside over our dances, if you love me; come and celebrate the nuptials of the gods, the banquets of us mortals and the festivals of the fortunate; these are the themes that inspire thy most poetic songs. And should Carcinus come to beg thee for admission with his sons to thy chorus,refuse all traffic with them; remember they are but gelded birds, stork-necked dancers, mannikins about as tall as a goat's turd, in fact machine-made poets. Contrary to all expectation, the father has at last managed to finish a piece, but he admits that a cat strangled it one fine evening.

sp.speaker: Second Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Such are the songs with which the Muse with the glorious hair inspires the able poet and which enchant the assembled populace, when the spring swallow twitters beneath the foliage; but the god spare us from the chorus of Morsimus and that of Melanthius! Oh! what a bitter discordancy grated upon my ears that day when the tragic chorus was directed by this same Melanthius and his brother, these two Gorgons, these two Harpies, the plague of the seas, whose gluttonous bellies devour the entire race of fishes, these followers of old women, these goats with their stinking arm-pits. Oh! Muse, spit upon them abundantly and keep the feast gaily with me.

div.stage: Trygaeus enters, limping painfully, accompanied by Opora and Theoria.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! it's a rough job getting to the gods! my legs are as good as broken through it. To the audience.How small you were, to be sure, when seen from heaven! you had all the appearance too of being great rascals; but seen close, you look even worse.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Is that you, master?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: So I've been told.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: What has happened to you?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: My legs pain me; it was such a dammed long journey.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Oh! tell me ...

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Did you see any other man besides yourself strolling about in heaven?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, only the souls of two or three dithyrambic poets.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: What were they doing up there?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: They were seeking to catch some lyric exordia as they flew by immersed in the billows of the air.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Is it true, what they tell us, that men are turned into stars after death?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Quite true.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: And who is the star over there now?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ion of Chios. The one who once wrote a poem about the dawn; as soon as he got up there, everyone called him the Morning Star.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: And those stars like sparks, that plough up the air as they dart across the sky?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: They are the rich leaving the feast with a lantern and a light inside it. —But hurry up, show this young girl into my house, pointing to Opora.clean out the bath, heat some water and prepare the nuptial couch for herself and me. When that's done, come back here; meanwhile I am off to present this other one to the Senate.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: But where then did you get these girls?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Where? why in heaven.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: I would not give more than an obolus for gods who have got to keeping brothels like us mere mortals.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: They are not all like that, but there are some up there too who live by this trade.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Come, that's rich! But tell me, shall I give her something to eat?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, for she would touch neither bread nor cake; she is used to licking ambrosia at the table of the gods.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Well, we can give her something to lick down here too.He takes Opora into the house.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Here is a truly happy old man, as far as I can judge.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! but what shall I be, when you see me presently dressed for the wedding?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Made young again by love and scented with perfumes, your lot will be one we all shall envy.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And when I lie beside her and fondle her breasts?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! then you will be happier than those spinning-tops who call Carcinus their father.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And I well deserve it; have I not bestridden a beetle to save the Greeks, who now, thanks to me, can make love at their ease and sleep peacefully on their farms?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: The girl has quitted the bath; she is charming from head to foot, belly and buttocks too; the cake is baked and they are kneading the sesame-biscuit;nothing is lacking but the bridegroom's tool.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us first hasten to lodge Theoria in the hands of the Senate.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Tell me, who is this woman?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why, it's the same Theoria.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: The one we used to go to Brauron with, to get tipsy and frolic?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You know, I could scarcely get hold of her.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Ah! you charmer! what pleasure your pretty bottom will afford me every four years!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let's see, which one of you is steady enough to be trusted by the Senate with the care of this charming wench?To the Servant. Hi! you, friend! what are you drawing there?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.stage: Who has been making signs in the air.
sp.p: It's er—well, at the Isthmian Games I shall have a tent for my tool.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, who wishes to take the charge of her? No one? Come, Theoria, I am going to lead you into the midst of the spectators and confide you to their care.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Ah! there is one who makes a sign to you.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Who is it?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: It's Ariphrades. He wishes to take her home at once.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, he must not. He would soon have her done for, absorbing all her life-force. Come, Theoria, take off all these clothes. Theoria undresses. As soon as she is nude, Trygaeus conducts her to the front row of seats, where the Senators sit.Senate, Prytanes, gaze upon Theoria and see what precious blessings I place in your hands. Hasten to raise its limbs and to immolate the victim. And look at this chimney.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: God, what a beautiful one! It's black with smoke because the Senate used to do its cooking there before the war.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Now that you have found Theoria again, you can start the most charming games from to-morrow, wrestling with her on the ground, on all fours, or you can lay her on her side, or stand before her with bent knees, or, well rubbed with oil, you can boldly enter the lists, as in the Pancratium, belaboring your foe with blows from your fist or something else. The next day you will celebrate equestrian games, in which the riders will ride side by side, or else the chariot teams, thrown one on top of another, panting and whinnying, will roll and knock against each other on the ground, while other rivals, thrown out of their seats, will fall before reaching the goal, utterly exhausted by their efforts. —Come, Prytanes, take Theoria. Oh! look how graciously yonder fellow has received her; you would not have been in such a hurry to introduce her to the Senate, if nothing were coming to you through it; you would not have failed to plead some holiday as an excuse.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Such a man as you assures the happiness of all his fellow-citizens.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: When you are gathering your vintages you will prize me even better.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: E'en from to-day we hail you as the deliverer of mankind.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Wait until you have drunk a beaker of new wine, before you appraise my true merits.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Excepting the gods, there is none greater than yourself, and that will ever be our opinion.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yea, Trygaeus of Athmonia has deserved well of you, he has freed both husbandman and craftsman from the most cruel ills; he has vanquished Hyberbolus.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Well then, what must be done now?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You must offer pots of green-stuff to the goddess to consecrate her altars.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Pots of green-stuff as we do to poor Hermes —and even he thinks the fare pretty mean?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What will you offer then? A fatted bull?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh no! I don't want to start bellowing the battle-cry.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: A great fat swine then?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: We don't want any of the swinishness of Theagenes.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What other victim do you prefer then?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: A sheep.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: A sheep?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Yes, by Zeus.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: But that's the Ionic form of the word.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Purposely. So that if anyone in the assembly says, “We must go to war,” all may start bleating in alarm, “Ba-ah, ba-ah!.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: A brilliant idea.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: And we shall all be lambs one toward the other, yes, and milder still toward the allies.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Then go for the sheep and haste to bring it back with you; I will prepare the altar for the sacrifice.They both leave.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: How everything succeeds to our wish, when the gods are willing and Fortune favours us! how opportunely everything falls out.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Nothing could be truer, for look! here stands the altar all ready at my door.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hurry, hurry, for the winds are fickle; make haste, while the divine will is set on stopping this cruel war and is showering on us the most striking benefits.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Here is the basket of barley-seed mingled with salt, the chaplet and the sacred knife; and there is the fire; so we are only waiting for the sheep.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hasten, hasten, for, if Chaeris sees you, he will come without bidding, he and his flute; and when you see him puffing and panting and out of breath, you will have to give him something.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.stage: to the Servant who has returned with a sheep and a vase of water.
sp.p: Come, seize the basket and take the lustral water and hurry to circle round the altar to the right.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: There! that's done. What is your next bidding?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Wait. I take this fire-brand first and plunge it into the water. Now quick, quick, you sprinkle the altar. Give me some barley-seed, purify yourself and hand me the basin; then scatter the rest of the barley among the audience.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Done.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You have thrown it?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Yes, by Hermes! and all the spectators have had their share.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: At least the women got none.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Oh! their husbands will give them some this evening.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us pray! Who is here? Are there any good men?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Come, give me the water, so that I may sprinkle these people. Faith! they are indeed good, brave men.

div.stage: He throws the lustral water on them.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You believe so?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: I am sure, and the proof of it is that we have flooded them with lustral water and they have not budged an inch.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us pray, then, as soon as we can.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Yes, let us pray.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! Peace, mighty queen, venerated goddess, thou, who presidest over choruses and at nuptials, deign to accept the sacrifices we offer thee.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Receive it, greatly honored mistress, and behave not like the courtesans, who half open the door to entice the gallants, draw back when they are stared at, to return once more if a man passes on. But do not thou act like this to us.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, but like an honest woman, show thyself to thy worshippers, who are worn with regretting thee all these thirteen years. Hush the noise of battle, be a true Lysimacha to us. Put an end to this tittle-tattle, to this idle babble, that set us defying one another. Cause the Greeks once more to taste the pleasant beverage of friendship and temper all hearts with the gentle feeling of forgiveness. Make excellent commodities flow to our markets, fine heads of garlic, early cucumbers, apples, pomegranates and nice little cloaks for the slaves; make them bring geese, ducks, pigeons and larks from Boeotia and baskets of eels from Lake Copais; we shall all rush to buy them, disputing their possession with Morychus, Teleas, Glaucetes and every other glutton. Melanthius will arrive on the market last of all; they'll say, “no more eels, all sold!” and then he'll start groaning and exclaiming as in his monologue of Medea, “I am dying, I am dying! Alas! I have let those hidden in the beet escape me!” And won't we laugh?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: These are the wishes, mighty goddess, which we pray thee to grant.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Take the knife and slaughter the sheep like a finished cook.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, the goddess does not wish it.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: And why not?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Blood cannot please Peace, so let us spill none upon her altar. Then go and sacrifice the sheep in the house, cut off the legs and bring them here; thus the carcass will be saved for the Choregus.The Servant goes into the house with the sheep.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: You, who remain here, get chopped wood and everything needed for the sacrifice ready.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Don't I look like a diviner preparing his mystic fire?

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Undoubtedly. Will anything that a wise man ought to know escape you? Don't you know all that a man should know, who is distinguished for his wisdom and inventive daring?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: There! the wood catches. Its smoke blinds poor Stilbides. I am now going to bring the table and thus be my own slave.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: You have braved a thousand dangers to save your sacred town. All honor to you! your glory will be ever envied.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Wait. Here are the legs, place them upon the altar. For myself, I mean to go back to the entrails and the cakes.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.stage: Going into the house ahead of the Servant.
sp.p: I'll take care of them. But I want you here.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Well then, here I am. Do you think I have taken long?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Just get this roasted. Ah! who is this man, crowned with laurel, who is coming to me?

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: He has a self-important look; is he some diviner?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, it's Hierocles, that oracle-monger from Oreus.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: What is he going to tell us?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Evidently he is coming to oppose the peace.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: No, it's the odor of the fat that attracts him.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let us appear not to see him.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: What sacrifice is this? to what god are you offering it?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Keep quiet.— Aloud.Look after the roasting and keep your hands off the meat.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: To whom are you sacrificing? Answer me.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! the tail is showing favourable omens.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: Aye, very favourable, oh, loved and mighty Peace!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Come, cut off the first offering and make the oblation.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: It's not roasted enough.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Yea, truly, it's done to a turn.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Mind your own business, friend! To the Servant.Cut away.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Where is the table?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Bring the libations.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: The tongue is cut separately.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: We know all that. But just listen to one piece of advice.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: And that is?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Don't talk, for it is divine Peace to whom we are sacrificing.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Oh! wretched mortals, oh, you idiots!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Keep such ugly terms for yourself.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: What! you are so ignorant you don't understand the will of the gods and you make a treaty, you, who are men, with apes, who are full of malice?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: What are you laughing at?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ha, ha! your apes amuse me!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: You simple pigeons, you trust yourselves to foxes, who are all craft, both in mind and heart.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh, you trouble-maker! may your lungs get as hot as this meat!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Nay, nay! if only the Nymphs had not fooled Bacis, and Bacis mortal men; and if the Nymphs had not tricked Bacis a second time ...

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: May the plague seize you, if you don't stop Bacizing!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: . . . it would not have been written in the book of Fate that the bonds of Peace must be broken; but first ...

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: The meat must be dusted with salt.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: . . . it does not please the blessed gods that we should stop the War until the wolf uniteth with the sheep.

div.stage: A kind of oracle-match now ensues.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: How, you cursed animal, could the wolf ever unite with the sheep?

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: As long as the wood-bug gives off a fetid odor, when it flies; as long as the noisy bitch is forced by nature to litter blind pups, so long shall peace be forbidden.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Then what should be done? Not to stop War would be to leave it to the decision of chance which of the two people should suffer the most, whereas by uniting under a treaty, we share the empire of Greece.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: You will never make the crab walk straight.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You shall no longer be fed at the Prytaneum; when the war is over oracles are not wanted.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: You will never smooth the rough spikes of the hedgehog.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Will you never stop fooling the Athenians?

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: What oracle ordered you to burn these joints of mutton in honor of the gods?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: This grand oracle of Homer's: “Thus vanished the dark war-clouds and we offered a sacrifice to new-born Peace. When the flame had consumed the thighs of the victim and its inwards had appeased our hunger, we poured out the libations of wine.” 'Twas I who arranged the sacred rites, but none offered the shining cup to the diviner.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: I care little for that. 'Tis not the Sibyl who spoke it.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Wise Homer has also said: “He who delights in the horrors of civil war has neither country nor laws nor home.” What noble words!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Beware lest the kite turn your brain and rob ...

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.stage: to the Servant who has returned with the libations.
sp.p: Look out, slave! This oracle threatens our meat. Quick, pour the libation, and give me some of the inwards.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: I too will help myself to a bit, if you like.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: The libation! the libation!

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Pour out also for me and give me some of this meat.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, the blessed gods won't allow it yet; let us drink; and as for you, get you gone, for that's their will. Mighty Peace! stay ever in our midst.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: Bring the tongue hither.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Relieve us of your own.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: The libation.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Here! and this into the bargain.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: You will not give me any meat?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: We cannot give you any until the wolf unites with the sheep.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: I will embrace your knees.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: 'Tis lost labour, good fellow; you will never smooth the rough spikes of the hedgehog.Come, spectators, join us in our feast.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: And what am I to do?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You? go and eat the Sibyl.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: No, by the Earth! no, you shall not eat without me; if you do not give, I shall take; it's common property.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Strike, strike this Bacis, this humbugging soothsayer.

sp.speaker: Hierocles
sp.p: I take to witness—

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And I also, that you are a glutton and an impostor. To the Servant.Hold him tight and I'll beat the impostor with a stick.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: You look to that; I will snatch the skin from him which he has stolen from us. Let go that skin, you priest from hell! do you hear! Oh! what a fine crow has come from Oreus! Won't you stretch your wings quickly for Elymnium?Hierocles flees. Trygaeus and the Servant go into the house.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! joy, joy! no more helmet, no more cheese nor onions! No, I have no passion for battles; what I love is to drink with good comrades in the corner by the fire when good dry wood, cut in the height of the summer, is crackling; it is to cook pease on the coals and beechnuts among the embers, it is to kiss our pretty Thracian while my wife is at the bath.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Nothing is more pleasing, when the rain is sprouting our sowings, than to chat with some friend, saying, “Tell me, Comarchides, what shall we do? I would willingly drink myself, while the heavens are watering our fields. Come, wife, cook three measures of beans, adding to them a little wheat, and give us some figs. Syra! call Manes off the fields, it's impossible to prune the vine or to align the ridges, for the ground is too wet today. Let someone bring me the thrush and those two finches; there were also some curds and four pieces of hare, unless the cat stole them last evening, for I know not what the infernal noise was that I heard in the house. Serve up three of the pieces for me, slave, and give the fourth to my father. Go and ask Aeschinades for some myrtle branches with berries on them,and then, for it's on the same road, invite Charinades

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: to come and drink with me to the honor of the gods who watch over our crops.”

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: When the grasshopper sings his dulcet tune, I love to see the Lemnian vines beginning to ripen, the earliest plant of all.Likewise I love to watch the fig filling out, and when it has reached maturity I eat it with appreciation, exclaiming, “Oh! delightful season!” Then too I bruise some thyme and infuse it in water. Indeed I grow a great deal fatter passing the summer in this way . . .

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: . . . than in watching a damned lieutenant with three plumes and military cloak of crimson, very livid indeed; he calls it the real Sardian purple, but if he ever has to fight in this cloak he'll dye it another color, the real Cyzicene yellow, he the first to run away, shaking his plumes like a buff hippalectryon, and I am left to do the real work. Once back again in Athens, these brave fellows behave abominably; they write down these, they scratch through others, and this backwards and forwards two or three times at random. The departure is set for to-morrow, and some citizen has brought no provisions, because he didn't know he had to go; he stops in front of the statue of Pandion, reads his name, is dumbfounded and starts away at a run, weeping bitter tears. The townsfolk are less ill-used, but that is how the husbandmen are treated by these men of war, the hated of the gods and of men, who know nothing but how to throw away their shield. For this reason, if it please heaven, I propose to call these rascals to account,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: for they are lions in times of peace, but sneaking foxes when it comes to fighting.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.stage: Coming out of his house, followed by the Servant.
sp.p: Oh! oh! what a crowd for the nuptial feast! Here! dust the tables with this crest, which is good for nothing else now. Halloa! produce the cakes, the thrushes, plenty of good jugged hare and the little loaves.

div.stage: A Sickle-maker enters with a comrade; one carries sickles, the other casks.

sp.speaker: Sickle-maker
sp.p: Trygaeus, where is Trygaeus?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I am cooking the thrushes.

sp.speaker: Sickle-maker
sp.p: Trygaeus, my best of friends, what a fine stroke of business you have done for me by bringing back Peace! Formerly my sickles would not have sold at an obolus apiece, to-day I am being paid fifty drachmae for every one. And here is a neighbor who is selling his casks for the country at three drachmae each. So come, Trygaeus, take as many sickles and casks as you will for nothing. Accept them for nothing; it's because of our handsome profits on our sales that we offer you these wedding presents.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Thanks. Put them all down inside there, and come along quick to the banquet. Ah! do you see that armorer yonder coming with a wry face?

div.stage: Enter an armorer, followed by other personages who represent the various specialized trades which have profited by the war, a crest-maker, a manufacturer of breastplates, a trumpet-maker, a helmet-maker, a polisher of lances; each carries a sample of his products. The armorer is the only one who speaks.

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: Alas! alas! Trygaeus, you have ruined me utterly.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What! won't the crests go any more, friend?

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: You have killed my business, my livelihood, and that of this poor lance-maker too.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, come, what are you asking for these two crests?

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: What do you bid for them?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: What do I bid? Oh! I am ashamed to say. Still, as the clasp is of good workmanship, I would give two, even three measures of dried figs; I could use them for dusting the table.

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: All right, tell them to bring me the dried figs. To the crest-maker.That's better than nothing, my friend.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Take them away, be off with your crests and get you gone; they are moulting, they are losing all their hair; I would not give a single fig for them.

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: Good gods, what am I going to do with this fine ten-mina breastplate, which is so splendidly made?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh, you will lose nothing over it. Sell it to me at cost price. It would be very useful as a thunder-mug ...

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: Cease your insults, both to me and my wares.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: ... if propped on three stones. He sits on it.Look, it's admirable.

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: But how can you wipe yourself, idiot?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: I can put one hand through here, and the other there, and so ...

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: What! do you wipe yourself with both hands?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Aye, so that I may not be accused of robbing the State, by blocking up an oar-hole in the galley.

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: Would you crap in a thunder-mug that cost ten minae?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Undoubtedly, you rascal. Do you think I would sell my arse for a thousand drachmae?

sp.speaker: Armourer
sp.p: Come, have the money paid over to me.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, friend; I find it pinches my bottom. Take it away, I won't buy it.

sp.speaker: Maker of War Trumpets
sp.p: What is to be done with this trumpet, for which I gave sixty drachmae the other day?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Pour lead into the hollow and fit a good, long stick to the top; and you will have a balanced cottabus.

sp.speaker: Maker of War Trumpets
sp.p: Don't mock me.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Well, here's another idea. Pour in lead as I said, add here a dish hung on strings, and you will have a balance for weighing the figs which you give your slaves in the fields.

sp.speaker: Helmet Maker
sp.p: Cursed fate! I am ruined. Here are helmets, for which I gave a mina each. What am I to do with them? who will buy them?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Go and sell them to the Egyptians; they will do for measuring laxatives.

sp.speaker: Spear Maker
sp.p: >Ah! poor helmet-maker, things are indeed in a bad way.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: He has no cause for complaint.

sp.speaker: Spear Maker
sp.p: But helmets will be no more used.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Let him learn to fit a handle to them and he can sell them for more money.

sp.speaker: Helmet Maker
sp.p: Let us be off, comrade.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: No, I want to buy these spears.

sp.speaker: Spear Maker
sp.p: What will you give?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: If they could be split in two, I would take them at a drachma per hundred to use as vine-props.

sp.speaker: Spear Maker
sp.p: The insolent dog! Let us go, friend.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Ah! here come the guests, young folks from the table to take a pee; I fancy they also want to hum over what they will be singing presently. Hi! child! what do you reckon to sing? Stand there and give me the opening line.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “Glory to the young warriors—”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! leave off about your young warriors, you little wretch; we are at peace and you are an idiot and a rascal.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “The skirmish begins, the hollow bucklers clash against each other.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Bucklers! Leave me in peace with your bucklers.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “And then there came groanings and shouts of victory.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Groanings! ah! by Bacchus! look out for yourself, you cursed squaller, if you start wearying us again with your groanings and hollow bucklers.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: Then what should I sing? Tell me what pleases you.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: “'Tis thus they feasted on the flesh of oxen,” or something similar, as, for instance, “Everything that could tickle the palate was placed on the table.”

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “'Tis thus they feasted on the flesh of oxen and, tired of warfare, unharnessed their foaming steeds.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: That's splendid; tired of warfare, they seat themselves at table; sing sing to us how they still go on eating after they are satiated.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “The meal over, they girded themselves—”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: With good wine, no doubt?

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: “—with armour and rushed forth from the towers, and a terrible shout arose.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Get you gone, you little scapegrace, you and your battles! You sing of nothing but warfare. Who is your father then?

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: My father?

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Yes, you, by Zeus.

sp.speaker: Son of Lamachus
sp.p: I am Lamachus' son.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Oh! oh! I could indeed have sworn, when I was listening to you, that you were the son of some warrior, who dreams of nothing but wounds and bruises, of some Bulomachus of Clausimachus; go and sing your plaguey songs to the spearmen.Where is the son of Cleonymus? Sing me something before going back to the feast. I am at least certain he will not sing of battles, for his father is far too careful a man.

sp.speaker: Son of Cleonymus
sp.p: “A Saian is parading with the spotless shield which I regret to say I have thrown into a thicket.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Tell me, you little good-for-nothing, are you singing that for your father?

sp.speaker: Son of Cleonymus
sp.p: “But I saved my life.”

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And dishonored your family. But let us go in; I am very certain, that being the son of such a father, you will never forget this song of the buckler.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You, who remain to the feast, it's your duty to devour dish after dish and not to ply empty jaws. Come, put heart into the work and eat with your mouths full. For, believe me, poor friends, white teeth are useless furniture if they chew nothing.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.stage: To Trygaeus, who is going into the house.
sp.p: Never fear; thanks all the same for your good advice.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: And all of you, who yesterday were dying of hunger, come, stuff yourselves with this fine hare-stew; it's not every day that we find cakes lying neglected. Eat, eat, or I predict you will soon regret it.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Silence! Keep silence! Here is the bride about to appear! Take nuptial torches and let all rejoice and join in our songs.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Then, when we have danced, clinked our cups and thrown Hyperbolus through the doorway we will carry back all our farming tools to the fields and shall pray the gods to give wealth to the Greeks and to cause us all to gather in an abundant barley harvest, enjoy a noble vintage, to grant that we may choke with good figs, that our wives may prove fruitful, that in fact we may recover all our lost blessings, and that the sparkling fire may be restored to the hearth.
sp.stage: Opora comes out of the house, followed by torch-bearing slaves.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Come, wife, to the fields and seek, my beauty, to brighten and enliven my nights.

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! thrice happy man, who so well deserve your good fortune!

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: What shall we do to her?

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: What shall we do to her?

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: We will gather her kisses.

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: We will gather her kisses.

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: But come, comrades, we who are in the first row, let us pick up the bridegroom and carry him in triumph.

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: You shall have a fine house,no cares and the finest of figs.

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: Second Half Chorus
sp.p: The bridegroom's fig is great and thick;

sp.speaker: First Half Chorus
sp.p: The bride's very soft and tender.

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: While eating and drinking deep draughts of wine, continue to repeat:

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus! Oh! Hymen! oh! Hymenaeus!

sp.speaker: Trygaeus
sp.p: Hail, hail, my friends. All who come with me shall have cakes galore.
